steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our short paper on data transfer optimizations between the host CPU and custom accelerators in AXI4MLIR. Motivate custom accelerators and the problem of writing host driver code, introduce AXI4MLIR, and explain the bottlenecks we observed that motivate our optimizations.

steps.text:
1. Custom hardware accelerators and the host driver challenge
2. Automated driver generation and AXI4MLIR
3. Observed inefficiencies and our proposed optimizations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Accelerators and drivers
- renewed interest in heterogeneous computing with custom accelerators: diminishing performance gains of traditional architectures, esp. as core count grows
- custom accelerators: performance via architectural-level support tailored to the problem/application
- tensor algebra: pervasive in machine learning; computationally demanding; high memory bandwidth -> specialized accelerators ideal
- challenge: realizing full potential needs efficient communication between accelerator, off-chip memory, host CPU -> hardware-software co-design of accelerator and host driver code
- driver: data transfers, synchronization, control via instructions / control signals
- manual driver code per accelerator and application: time-consuming, error-prone

2. AXI4MLIR
- automated CPU-accelerator driver code generation: considers host-CPU, accelerator, communication protocol, available instructions
- AXI4MLIR: extension of MLIR compiler framework; generates host-driver code offloading linear algebra ops to custom AXI-Stream accelerators
- input: high-level app description in MLIR linalg abstraction; custom MLIR attributes describe accelerator capabilities; lowered to DMA library calls sending/receiving data and instructions

3. Motivation for optimizations
- considerable speedup over manual host-driver code, but room to improve accelerator utilization and overall latency
- Figure 1: breakdown of cycles inside accelerator, MatMul, range of dimensions and tile sizes
- ideally compute cores fully utilized; observed less than 10% utilization on average
- CPU-side profiling: bottleneck = copying heap-allocated data to DMA buffers
- propose extending AXI4MLIR with three key optimizations (next section)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There is renewed interest in heterogeneous computing with custom hardware accelerators, and this is because the performance improvements of traditional architectures are diminishing, especially when the core count grows. Custom hardware accelerators give more performance through architectural-level support that is tailored to what the specific problem or application needs. Tensor algebra processing is everywhere in machine learning applications, and it is computationally demanding and needs high memory bandwidth. Specialized accelerators are ideal to give the computational power that these applications need. But using custom accelerators brings a new challenge, which is how to realize their full potential. This needs efficient communication between the accelerator, off-chip memory, and the host CPU, so it needs effective hardware-software co-design of the accelerator and the host driver code. An efficient accelerator driver is needed to handle data transfers, synchronize operations, and control the accelerator with instructions or control signals. However, developing host driver code by hand for a particular accelerator and for different applications takes a lot of time and is error-prone.

To solve this problem we can use automated generation of CPU-accelerator driver code, which takes into account the host-CPU, the accelerator, the communication protocol used, and the accelerator instructions that are available. AXI4MLIR is an extension of the MLIR compiler framework. It generates host-driver code that offloads linear algebra operations to custom accelerators based on AXI-Stream. AXI4MLIR takes as input a high-level description of the application in MLIR’s linear algebra (linalg) abstraction, and it introduces custom MLIR attributes to describe what the target accelerator can do. In the end these get transformed into low-level DMA library calls that send or receive data and instructions to the accelerator.

Motivation for optimizations
- considerable speedup over manual host-driver code, but room to improve accelerator utilization and overall latency
- Figure 1: breakdown of cycles inside accelerator, MatMul, range of dimensions and tile sizes
- ideally compute cores fully utilized; observed less than 10% utilization on average
- CPU-side profiling: bottleneck = copying heap-allocated data to DMA buffers
- propose extending AXI4MLIR with three key optimizations (next section)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There is renewed interest in heterogeneous computing with custom hardware accelerators, and this is because the performance improvements of traditional architectures are diminishing, especially when the core count grows. Custom hardware accelerators give more performance through architectural-level support that is tailored to what the specific problem or application needs. Tensor algebra processing is everywhere in machine learning applications, and it is computationally demanding and needs high memory bandwidth. Specialized accelerators are ideal to give the computational power that these applications need. But using custom accelerators brings a new challenge, which is how to realize their full potential. This needs efficient communication between the accelerator, off-chip memory, and the host CPU, so it needs effective hardware-software co-design of the accelerator and the host driver code. An efficient accelerator driver is needed to handle data transfers, synchronize operations, and control the accelerator with instructions or control signals. However, developing host driver code by hand for a particular accelerator and for different applications takes a lot of time and is error-prone.

To solve this problem we can use automated generation of CPU-accelerator driver code, which takes into account the host-CPU, the accelerator, the communication protocol used, and the accelerator instructions that are available. AXI4MLIR is an extension of the MLIR compiler framework. It generates host-driver code that offloads linear algebra operations to custom accelerators based on AXI-Stream. AXI4MLIR takes as input a high-level description of the application in MLIR’s linear algebra (linalg) abstraction, and it introduces custom MLIR attributes to describe what the target accelerator can do. In the end these get transformed into low-level DMA library calls that send or receive data and instructions to the accelerator.

AXI4MLIR can give considerable speedup compared to a manual implementation of the host-driver code, but we see some areas where it could be optimized further, which can improve how well the accelerator is utilized and reduce the overall latency. Figure 1 shows a breakdown of the cycles spent inside the accelerator when executing MatMul problems for a range of dimensions and tile sizes. Ideally the compute cores of the accelerator should be fully utilized, but in our experiments we get less than 10% utilization on average. We also profiled the execution of this MatMul problem from the point of view of the CPU, and we saw that the bottleneck on the CPU side comes from copying data allocated in the memory heap to the DMA buffers. To deal with this under-utilization of the accelerator and the bottlenecks on the host side, we propose to extend AXI4MLIR with three key optimizations, which are discussed in detail in the next section.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Renewed interest in heterogeneous computing with custom hardware accelerators can be attributed to the diminishing performance improvements of traditional architectures, especially as the core count grows. Custom hardware accelerators provide increased performance through architectural-level support tailored to the specific requirements of the given problem or application [1,2,3,4]. Tensor algebra processing, which is pervasive in machine learning [5] applications, is computationally demanding and requires high memory bandwidth, and specialized accelerators are ideal for providing the computational power these applications need. Leveraging custom accelerators poses a new challenge - how do we realize their full potential? This requires efficient communication between the accelerator, off-chip memory, and host CPU, demanding effective hardware-software co-design of the accelerator and host driver code. An efficient accelerator driver is necessary to handle data transfers, synchronize operations, and control the accelerator with instructions or control signals. However, manually developing host driver code for a particular accelerator and different applications is a very time-consuming and error-prone process.

To solve this problem, we can use automated CPU-accelerator driver code generation that considers the host-CPU, the accelerator, the associated communication protocol, and the available accelerator instructions. AXI4MLIR [6] is an extension of the MLIR compiler framework [7] that generates host-driver code which offloads linear algebra operations to custom AXI-Stream based accelerators. AXI4MLIR takes as input a high-level application description in MLIR’s linear algebra (linalg) abstraction [8] and introduces custom MLIR attributes to describe the capabilities of the target accelerator, which are eventually transformed into low-level DMA library calls that send or receive data and instructions to the accelerator.

While AXI4MLIR can provide considerable speedup over a manual implementation of the host-driver code, we observe potential areas for further optimization that can improve the utilization of the accelerator and reduce overall latency. Figure 1 shows a breakdown of the cycles spent inside the accelerator while executing MatMul problems for a range of dimensions and tile sizes. Ideally, the accelerator’s compute cores should be fully utilized, but our experiments show on average less than 10% utilization. Additionally, when profiling the execution of this MatMul problem from the CPU’s perspective, we observed that the CPU-side bottleneck is caused by copying data allocated within the memory heap to the DMA buffers. To tackle this accelerator under-utilization and these host-side bottlenecks, we propose extending AXI4MLIR with three key optimizations, discussed in detail in the following section.
